title: What IS Debate?
subtitle: Orientation · Mission 01
tagline: Policy debate is a {{cyan:game}}. Two teams, one judge, one big rule to argue about. Learn the players, the prize, and the rules of the {{amber:arena}}.

slides.headline: 🎮 ENTER THE ARENA
body: You and your best friend can't agree: *should your school ban phones?*
You both feel **strongly**. Neither of you is backing down. How do you settle it without just yelling louder?
That's what {{cyan: policy debate}} does. It gives you {{amber: rules}}, a {{amber: timer}}, and a judge — so you can win an argument with your {{cyan:brain}}, not your volume.
Today: meet the game, meet the players, meet the prize. 🏆

items.label: Define {{cyan: policy debate}} as an academic game
Tell apart the {{cyan: Affirmative}}, the {{amber: Negative}}, and the Judge
Spot a {{cyan: resolution}} and pick which side argues for it

slides.definition: {{cyan: Policy debate}} is an academic **game**. Two teams of two argue about whether one big {{cyan: rule}} should change. A judge keeps score and picks the winner. 🎮
slides.plainWords: Not a fight. Not yelling. A *game* with sides, a timer, and a referee. You play to win — and you win with your brain.
slides.analogy: Think of it like a {{cyan: video game}}. Two players per team. A clock on every move. A scoreboard. And a {{amber: boss fight}} at the end of the tournament: the trophy. 🏆

slides.headline: MEET THE PLAYERS
slides.intro: Every policy debate round has three roles. Two teams play. One judge calls the winner. Here's who does what.

cards.name: AFFIRMATIVE
cards.description: The {{cyan: YES team}}. They say *change the rule.* They bring a {{cyan: plan}} to fix the problem.

example.label: Sounds like
example.text: "Yes, schools should ban phones — and here's our plan to do it."

cards.name: NEGATIVE
cards.description: The {{amber: NO team}}. They defend things the way they are now. They prove the Aff's plan is {{amber: a bad idea}}.

example.label: Sounds like
example.text: "No, keep things the way they are — the Aff's plan will only make it worse."

cards.name: THE JUDGE
cards.description: One neutral grown-up. They listen to {{cyan: both sides}}, track every point, and sign the ballot for the team that argued best.

example.label: Sounds like
example.text: "I voted Aff. They proved the plan solves the problem and the Neg never beat that point."

slides.headline: 🤝 HOUSE RULES OF THE ARENA
slides.intro: Debate isn't a free-for-all. There are three rules every debater plays by. Break them and you don't just lose the round — you lose the room.

rows.name: 🎤 Never interrupt a speech
rows.description: When the other team is up, you {{cyan: listen}} and take notes. You'll get your turn. Every speech has a timer — the clock is the only thing that can cut someone off.

counter.label: Why it works
counter.text: Judges *hate* rude debaters. The team that listens calmly looks like the team in control — even before they speak.

rows.name: 🫱 Respect the other team
rows.description: You can {{cyan: attack the argument}} as hard as you want. You never attack the person. No name-calling. No eye-rolls. {{amber: Argue the idea, not the kid.}}

counter.label: Why it works
counter.text: Calling out a *bad argument* is sharp. Calling out a *bad person* makes you look small. Sharp wins ballots; small loses them.

rows.name: 💪 Try your hardest, even when it's hard
rows.description: Some rounds will feel rough. The topic is tricky, the other team is fast, your brain is tired. You {{cyan: keep going}} anyway. That's how debaters grow.

counter.label: Why it works
counter.text: Every great debater lost a *lot* of rounds before they started winning. The ones who stuck with it got good. The ones who quit didn't.

prompt.label: QUICK CHECK
prompt.question: 👥 How many people are on one policy debate team?

correct.title: ✓ TARGET ACQUIRED
body: Locked in. Policy debate is **2 vs 2**. You and your {{cyan: debate partner}} are a team — you split the speeches and back each other up the whole round.
correct.followup: **Pro move:** A great team plays like *one brain in two bodies*. When your partner speaks, you're already prepping their next move.

a.title: ✕ NOT SOLO
body: Policy debate isn't a one-person game. You always have a {{cyan: debate partner}} — **two players per team**, four people total in the round.

c.title: ✕ NOT THREE
body: Close, but it's {{cyan: two}}. Every policy debate team is exactly **2 people** — you and your partner.

d.title: ✕ THAT'S BOTH TEAMS TOGETHER
body: Four is the *whole round* — two on Aff, two on Neg. One team is just {{cyan: two}}.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: The answer is {{cyan: B — 2}}. You always have a debate partner.

prompt.label: PATTERN MATCH
prompt.scenario: Match each player to what they do in the round.
prompt.question: Drag from the left to its match on the right.

items.text: Says YES — change the rule. Brings a plan.
Says NO — keep things the way they are.
Listens to both sides and picks the winner.

correct.title: ✓ ROLES LOCKED IN
body: Clean match. {{cyan: Aff}} says yes and brings a plan. {{amber: Neg}} says no and defends what we already do. The Judge picks the team that argued best.
correct.followup: **Pro move:** Before every round, ask yourself one question: *which side am I on this round?* You'll argue {{cyan: both}} sides this summer — sometimes in the same day.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ ROLES CROSSED
body: Use this trick: {{cyan: Aff = AFFIRM = YES}}. {{amber: Neg = NEGATE = NO}}. The Judge is the only one who isn't on a team.

prompt.label: FIELD READ
prompt.scenario:
The topic is: *"Our school should ban cell phones during lunch."*

Team A argues: *"Yes, ban phones — it'll stop bullying online."* 📵
Team B argues: *"No, keep phones — kids need them for emergencies."* 📱
prompt.question: Which team is the AFFIRMATIVE?

options.text: Team A — they want the rule to change
Team B — they want things to stay the same

correct.title: ✓ CLEAN HIT
body: Right. {{cyan: Team A}} wants the rule to change → they're the **Affirmative**. Team B wants to keep things the way they are → they're the **Negative**.
correct.followup: **Memory trick:** The {{cyan: Aff}} *affirms* the resolution. If the resolution says "ban phones," the Aff says **YES, ban them**. The Neg says **NO, don't**.

b.title: ✕ FLIPPED
body: Team B wants things to stay the *same* — that's the {{amber: Negative}}. The team that wants the rule to **change** (Team A) is the Aff.

c.title: ✕ ONLY ONE SIDE IS AFF
body: Both teams argue, true — but only one team is the {{cyan: Affirmative}}. The Aff is the team that says **YES** to the resolution. That's Team A here.

d.title: ✕ THE JUDGE DOESN'T ARGUE
body: The judge only picks the winner — they don't take a side. The {{cyan: Aff}} is the team **arguing for** the rule change. That's Team A.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: The answer is {{cyan: A}}. The Aff is the team that wants the rule to change. Team A wants to ban phones, so they're the Aff.

prompt.label: JUDGE'S EYES
prompt.scenario: You're the judge. 🧑‍⚖️ Sort each move into how it'd look on your ballot.
prompt.question: Drop each action into the right bin.

cards.text: Taking notes while the other team speaks 📝
Making eye contact with the judge 👀
Cutting off the other team's speech 🗣️
Trying hard even when you're behind 💪

correct.title: ✓ JUDGE'S EYES TRAINED
body: Clean sort. The {{cyan: good moves}} all have one thing in common: they treat the round like a {{cyan: game}}, not a fight. The {{amber: bad moves}} all do the opposite — they break the rules and burn the judge's patience.
correct.followup: **Pro move:** Judges decide *partly* on arguments and *partly* on **vibe**. A calm, kind debater who tries hard wins close rounds. A rude one loses them.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISALIGNED
body: Litmus test: ask {{cyan: "Would the judge nod or frown?"}} Note-taking, eye contact, and effort = nods. Name-calling, interrupting, and giving up = frowns.

prompt.scenario: Fill in the missing words to describe a policy debate round.
prompt.question: Drop the right word into each blank.

slides.template: Policy debate is a game played by two teams of two. The {{1}} team argues YES — change the rule. The {{2}} team argues NO — keep things the way they are. A neutral {{3}} listens to both sides and picks the winner.

blanks.hint: The YES team — the one that wants the rule to change
The NO team — the one defending what we already do
The neutral person who picks the winner

correct.title: ✓ ROUND ASSEMBLED
body: That's the whole game in three words: {{cyan: Affirmative}}, {{amber: Negative}}, and {{cyan: Judge}}. Memorize them. You'll use them every single round this summer.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ REBUILD
body: Three checkpoints: {{cyan: Affirmative}} = YES, change the rule. {{amber: Negative}} = NO, keep things the same. {{cyan: Judge}} = the neutral grown-up who picks the winner.

prompt.label: BIG IDEA CHECK
prompt.question: 🎯 What makes policy debate **different** from arguing with your friend at lunch?

options.text: Debate has rules, a timer, and a judge — lunch arguments don't
Debate is always about lunch food
There's no real difference — both are just arguing

correct.title: ✓ THAT'S THE WHOLE GAME
body: Exactly. A lunch argument is whoever talks loudest. A {{cyan: debate round}} has a timer, sides, and a referee — so the team with the best *thinking* wins, not the team with the biggest mouth. 🧠
correct.followup: **Pro tip:** This is *why* shy kids often become **great** debaters. The rules level the playing field. You don't need to be the loudest — you need to be the **clearest**.

b.title: ✕ NOT THE TOPIC
body: Policy debate can be about almost anything — phones, recess, school start times, big national rules. The thing that makes it *debate* isn't the topic. It's the {{cyan: rules}}, {{cyan: timer}}, and {{cyan: judge}}.

c.title: ✕ LOUDER ISN'T BETTER
body: Actually, the {{amber: opposite}}. Yelling loses rounds. The team with rules on their side — clear arguments, calm voice, eye contact — wins.

d.title: ✕ THERE'S A BIG DIFFERENCE
body: A lunch argument has no referee and no clock. A {{cyan: debate round}} has both — plus sides, plans, and a judge keeping score. That structure is what makes it a game.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: The answer is {{cyan: A}}. Debate has {{cyan: rules}}, a {{cyan: timer}}, and a {{cyan: judge}}. That's what makes it a game and not a yelling match.

slides.headline: ARENA: CLEARED ✅
slides.subtext: You now know the game. Two teams of two. {{cyan: Aff}} says YES. {{amber: Neg}} says NO. The Judge picks the winner. House rules: listen, respect, try hard. You're ready for the arena. 🎮
